query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In oxide-forming high‐entropy alloys, resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion is governed by an adaptive passivation mechanism in which a rapidly regenerating protective oxide/spinel film continuously reforms after mechanical removal, thereby mitigating combined degradation more effectively than the sum of isolated wear and corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: A multiprincipal-element HEA with a homogeneous single-phase solid solution microstructure that is predisposed to in situ formation of a passivating oxide film.
generation.intervention: Fabricate two matched HEA samples by alloy composition tuning: one alloy containing key oxide-forming elements (e.g., Cr or Mn) and a baseline alloy lacking these elements, while keeping all other processing and microstructural parameters constant.
generation.conditions: Expose both alloys to simultaneous mechanical wear (e.g., controlled sliding or abrasion) and a corrosive environment (chloride-rich aqueous solution) at temperatures that favor oxide film formation.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and rapid regeneration of a protective oxide/spinel film at the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Under combined mechanical and corrosive stresses, the protective oxide film is intermittently removed by wear. In alloys with oxide-forming elements, the available elements facilitate rapid re-formation of the film, thus minimizing further damage by preventing continuous exposure to the corrosive medium. In contrast, the absence of these elements in the baseline alloy results in degradation that more closely matches the additive effects of isolated wear and corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: The oxide-forming HEA will exhibit lower overall degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion conditions than the baseline alloy. Specifically, measurements will show wear and corrosion rates that are synergistically reduced (i.e., the combined degradation is less than the sum of its isolated components) in the presence of an adaptive, self-healing oxide film.
generation.baseline: A compositionally similar HEA that lacks the critical oxide-forming elements necessary for rapid passivation.
generation.boundary: This prediction is expected to hold when the mechanical removal rate does not exceed the film’s regeneration capability and when environmental conditions (e.g., temperature, chloride concentration) support oxide film formation; if wear becomes too aggressive or conditions inhibit film formation, the adaptive passivation mechanism may fail.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative measures of wear-corrosion synergy and the limits of oxide regeneration kinetics relative to wear rate remain to be fully determined and may vary with specific alloy compositions and environmental parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two HEA specimens with identical microstructures and processing histories, differing only in the inclusion (adaptive alloy) or omission (baseline alloy) of key oxide-forming elements. Subject both specimens to a simultaneous tribocorrosion test by applying controlled sliding abrasion in a chloride-rich aqueous solution at a temperature that enables oxide formation.
measurements: Quantify mass loss and wear volume over time
Measure corrosion current density and potential via electrochemical tests
Characterize the nature and thickness of the surface oxide film using surface analytical techniques (e.g., XPS, SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the adaptive alloy (with oxide formers) does not show a statistically significant reduction in combined degradation (i.e., its mass loss, wear, and corrosion rates are similar to or exceed those of the baseline, and no evidence of a self-healing oxide film is observed), then the hypothesis of an adaptive, passivating film governing wear-corrosion resistance is falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a new approach of alloying concepts. Whereas conventional alloys usually comprise one major alloying element and minor additions of other alloying elements to improve properties, HEAs consist of at least five elements with close to equimolar composition. For several compositions, the desired formation of solely solid solutions with a face-centred cubic (fcc) or a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure could be achieved [ [1] , [2] , [3] ].

Several groups of HEAs have been intensively investigated. The term compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) was introduced for HEAs with a multiphase microstructure [ [4] ]. Several investigations prove the formation of primarily cubic phases in the alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi and its derivatives [ [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Aluminium strongly influences the microstructure, phase formation and resulting properties. Furthermore, aluminium acts as a stabiliser of bcc solid solutions and can suppress the formation of complex phases [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm

frame.system: High-entropy alloy (HEA) systems engineered for harsh, corrosive, and mechanically demanding environments. The starting state is a multiprincipal-element alloy with a microstructure that potentially forms adaptive, passivating surface films during exposure.
frame.goal: To establish a single mechanistic hypothesis that explains the HEA’s resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, thereby understanding the interplay (synergy) between mechanical degradation and chemical attack.
frame.limitation: There is currently no unified, mechanistic understanding of how the dynamic interplay between wear and corrosion governs degradation in HEAs. Existing studies have separately addressed wear or corrosion, but the synergy in combined environments remains unclear.
constraints: Hypothesis must be singular and mechanistic, unifying the effect of both wear (mechanical removal) and corrosion (chemical degradation)
A controlled comparison is required that tests the hypothesis versus a matched baseline (e.g., similar alloy without the presumed adaptive mechanism)
The experimental design must predict distinct differences between combined degradation and isolated wear or corrosion components
Clearly define conditions under which the prediction holds true, fails, or is falsified
frame.regime: Test conditions featuring simultaneous mechanical stress (e.g., sliding, abrasion) in a corrosive medium (e.g., chloride-rich aqueous environment, potentially under elevated temperatures) that mimic service conditions in harsh industrial applications.
prior_attempts: Previous studies have examined wear resistance and corrosion resistance in HEAs independently, or in conventional alloys in a tribocorrosion context; however, they failed to integrate these degradation modes into a single mechanistic framework. The lack of a controlled, matched comparison limited the ability to discern synergy effects.

decision.trend: Earlier HEA studies typically addressed wear and corrosion as separate phenomena. For example, PMC7515071 investigated wear behavior under high-temperature reciprocating conditions and observed the formation of protective spinel phases, while PMC7866258 varied processing conditions to optimize both wear and corrosion resistance. Although these works demonstrated that microstructural features and processing choices could enhance individual properties, none unified the phenomena into a singular, mechanistic framework. The trend shows an evolution from isolated tests toward recognizing that under simultaneous degradation conditions, adaptive passivation (via in situ formed oxide/spinel films) might counteract wear. However, the dynamic interplay between mechanical removal and rapid film regeneration remains insufficiently understood.
decision.unsolved: The key unresolved question is how an adaptive passivation mechanism—where a protective oxide or spinel film forms and regenerates to offset material loss from mechanical wear—governs overall tribocorrosion resistance in HEAs. It is unclear under what conditions the film can keep pace with wear and how its formation is influenced by high-entropy composition and diffusion kinetics. Furthermore, the exact compositional and microstructural triggers for this synergy remain unconfirmed.
decision.lever: Alloy composition tuning: fabricate matched HEA systems with and without critical oxide-forming elements (e.g., Cr or Mn) that are hypothesized to drive adaptive passivation under simultaneous wear and corrosion conditions
decision.why: This approach follows the trend toward integrating wear and corrosion mechanisms by directly testing the role of adaptive film formation. By comparing a HEA with a complete set of oxide-forming elements against a baseline alloy missing these elements—under identical simultaneous mechanical and corrosive stresses—the experiment can reveal if rapid film regeneration mitigates combined degradation. If the alloy lacking the oxide-forming element shows no such synergy (i.e., degradation equal to the sum of isolated wear and corrosion effects), it would falsify the adaptive passivation hypothesis.
